chapter.name: A Story of Numbers
chapter.blurb: How number systems evolved: counting by one-to-one mapping, early systems using body parts, tallies and counting in twos, Roman landmark numbers, the Egyptian system and the idea of a base, and the place value systems that led to the Hindu number system with its zero.

scope_in.item: Count a collection by making a one-to-one mapping between it and a standard sequence of objects, names or symbols taken in order
State what a collection must have to serve as a number system: a fixed order and an unending sequence, and name the symbols of a written system as numerals
Compare the stick, letter-sound and written-symbol methods of counting and give the advantage and the drawback of each
Recognise tally marks as one mark per object, and the Lebombo bone (29 notches, about 44,000 years old) and the Ishango bone as the oldest known tally records
Read and extend the Gumulgal way of counting in twos, where urapon is 1, ukasar is 2 and any number above 6 was called ras, and compare it with the Bakairi and Bushmen systems
Explain why counting in groups of a fixed size (commonly 2, 5, 10 or 20) is more efficient than a tally, and relate it to the limit of about four objects seen at a glance
Write and read Roman numerals using the landmark symbols I, V, X, L, C, D and M, grouping the number largest landmark first, including the shorter forms IV and XL
Add two Roman numerals by collecting like symbols and regrouping them, and explain why multiplication and division are hard in this system
Recognise the Egyptian landmark numbers as the powers of 10 and represent a number such as 324 or 10458 by grouping it into them
Build a base-5 system in the same way and represent numbers such as 143 and 651 in it by grouping into 1, 5, 25, 125 and 625
State the definition of a base-n number system (first landmark number 1, each next one n times the current) and give its landmark numbers as the powers of n
Add in a base system by regrouping ten of one landmark number into one of the next, as in 15 tens and 15 units making 165
Use the fact that the product of two landmark numbers of a base system is another landmark number, with the distributive property, to multiply a numeral by a landmark number
Read a number on the decimal abacus, where each line is a power of 10 and a counter above a line counts 5, and carry ten counters on a line to the next line
State the shortcoming of the Egyptian system: higher and higher powers of 10 each need a brand new symbol
Group a number into powers of 60 and write it in the Mesopotamian base-60 place value system, as with 640, 7530 and 3605
Explain why an empty position needs a placeholder symbol, and what ambiguity remained because the Mesopotamians did not use it at the end of a numeral
Read a Mayan numeral from its landmark positions 1, 20 and 360, with dot for 1, bar for 5 and shell for 0, and say why it is only almost a base-20 system
Read a Chinese rod numeral by its landmark number positions, e.g. 2, 6, 3, 4 reading as 2634
State the features of the Hindu number system: base 10, ten digits, place value, and 0 used both as a placeholder and as a number in its own right
Form a place value system in another base, such as a base-2 system using two words as digits, and write small numbers in it

scope_out.item: Converting a number from one base to another by repeated division and remainders
scope_out.reason: The chapter converts only by grouping into landmark numbers largest first; no division algorithm is taught

scope_out.item: Binary arithmetic, bitwise working or hexadecimal numbers
scope_out.reason: Base 2 appears once, only as a place value writing exercise on p. 80, and nothing is computed in it

scope_out.item: Sexagesimal fractions, and fractions in any non-decimal base
scope_out.reason: The chapter states explicitly on p. 70 that it will not go into how the Mesopotamians represented fractions

scope_out.item: The laws of exponents, such as adding powers when multiplying
scope_out.reason: Powers of 10 and of n appear here only as names for landmark numbers; the laws themselves belong to Chapter 2, Power Play

scope_out.item: Roman numerals above 3999, the overbar for thousands, and the modern strict subtractive rules
scope_out.reason: The largest Roman symbol given is M, and the chapter records that writers were not consistent, e.g. 40 written as both XL and XXXX

scope_out.item: Placing the civilisations in chronological order, or treating each system as an improvement on the one before it
scope_out.reason: The chapter states on pp. 51 and 60 that the systems are presented in order of ideas, not of history, and warns against this reading

scope_out.item: Reading and writing large numbers with the Indian and international place value charts, periods and commas
scope_out.reason: The chapter is about how place value came about, not about naming lakhs and crores or grouping digits

scope_out.item: Egyptian fractions, and Egyptian methods of multiplication by doubling
scope_out.reason: Only whole-number grouping and multiplication by a landmark number are shown, on pp. 66-68

scope_out.item: Writing the actual Egyptian, Mesopotamian, Mayan or Chinese glyphs from memory
scope_out.reason: The glyphs appear only as pictures in the book; what is assessed is the grouping and the place values behind them

concepts.name: Counting and the idea of a number system
concepts.description: One-to-one mapping as the mechanism of counting, and what a collection of objects, names or symbols must have before it can serve as a number system.
concepts.idea: To count a collection you pair its objects, one by one, with a standard sequence that everyone agrees on and that never runs out.
concepts.rule: A number system is a standard sequence of objects, names or written symbols with a fixed order. Counting a collection means making a one-to-one mapping between the collection and that sequence, taken in order.
concepts.example: Keeping one stick for every cow in the herd tells you at once whether a cow is missing, without using any number names at all.

questions.q: Giving every cow in a herd exactly one stick, so that no two cows are given the same stick, is called a
questions.a: one-to-one mapping

questions.q: A standard sequence of objects, names or written symbols that has a fixed order and is used for counting is called a ____.
questions.a: number system

questions.q: The written symbols that represent numbers in a written number system are called
questions.a: numerals

questions.q: In Method 2 the sounds of the 26 English letters a to z are used as the standard sequence. The largest collection this can count is one of
questions.a: 26 objects

questions.q: Why is the stick system of Method 1 inconvenient for counting a large herd?
questions.a: One stick must be kept for every animal, so a large herd needs a huge pile of sticks
o: One stick must be kept for every animal, so a large herd needs a huge pile of sticks
The sticks run out once the herd passes 26
Sticks cannot be paired one to one with animals
The stick system cannot count past 20

questions.q: What is the drawback of the written system of Method 3, in which 1 to 20 are written I, II, III, IV, V and so on?
questions.a: Writing larger and larger numbers needs more and more new symbols
o: Writing larger and larger numbers needs more and more new symbols
Its symbols have no fixed order
It cannot be written down, only spoken

questions.q: Method 1 counts with sticks and Method 2 counts with the sounds of the 26 letters a to z. Give one advantage and one drawback of each.
questions.a: The stick sequence never runs out, but a large collection needs as many sticks as there are objects. The letter sequence is quick and easy to say, but it stops at 26, so it cannot count a larger collection.
s: Sticks: the sequence never ends, but as many sticks are needed as there are objects
Letters: convenient to say in order, but the sequence stops at 26

questions.q: A number system has to be an unending standard sequence because
questions.a: there is no end to numbers, so counting must never be forced to stop
o: there is no end to numbers, so counting must never be forced to stop
every collection has more than 26 objects
the Hindu number system uses ten digits
sticks and pebbles are difficult to carry about

questions.q: Which statement about numerals is correct?
questions.a: 36 and 193 are numerals of the Hindu number system
o: 36 and 193 are numerals of the Hindu number system
A numeral is the name that is spoken for a number
Only a single symbol such as 5 can be a numeral
Numerals are the sticks kept for the objects being counted

questions.q: The letters a to z stand for 1 to 26, and the system is then extended so that aa is 27, bb is 28, cc is 29 and so on. In this extension the string dd stands for ____.
A shepherd drops one pebble into a pot as each sheep leaves and takes one out as each sheep returns. At the end three pebbles are still in the pot. This tells him that
questions.a: three sheep have not returned
o: three extra sheep have joined the flock
the flock has three sheep in all
three pebbles were lost while counting

questions.q: Reema has one stick for each of her cows and her neighbour has one stick for each of his. Without using any number names, explain how she can tell whether she has fewer cows than he does, and how many more she would need to have as many as he has.
questions.a: She pairs her sticks with his, one to one, until one collection runs out. If hers runs out first she has fewer cows, and the sticks left over in his collection are exactly the number of extra cows she would need.
s: Pairs the two collections of sticks one to one until one runs out
Whichever collection runs out first has fewer, and the leftover sticks are the number still needed

questions.q: Using only collections of sticks, and no number names or Hindu numerals, give a method for adding two collections and a method for subtracting one from the other.
questions.a: To add, push both collections together into one pile; the combined pile is the sum. To subtract, take away from the first collection one stick for every stick of the second; what is left is the difference.
s: Addition: put both collections together, and the combined collection is the sum
Subtraction: remove one stick of the first for each stick of the second, and the remainder is the difference

questions.q: Rahul counts a basket of mangoes by touching each mango once and saying a, b, c, ... in order, and stops on the letter q. How many mangoes are in the basket?

A trader has to keep records of herds of up to 500 animals. Explain why the stick system and the 26-letter system both fail him, and state the property a number system must have so that it does not fail.
questions.a: The stick system would need up to 500 sticks for a single herd, which is impossible to carry or compare. The 26-letter system stops at 26, so it cannot name 500 at all. A usable number system must be an unending sequence with a fixed order whose representations stay short enough to write and read.
s: Sticks: up to 500 sticks would be needed for one herd, so the record is unmanageable
Letters: the sequence ends at 26, so 500 cannot be named at all
A number system must be unending, fixed in order, and short to write

questions.q: Assertion (A): The sounds of the 26 English letters, used as in Method 2, do not make a satisfactory number system. Reason (R): The sequence a to z has a fixed order.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q: Consider: (I) Counting a collection means making a one-to-one mapping between it and a standard sequence taken in order. (II) A number system has to be made of written symbols. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Only I

questions.q: Two children count the same row of 12 shells. One reaches 12, the other touches one shell twice and reaches 13. Name the rule of counting the second child broke, explain what went wrong, and say how counting with sticks would have shown the mistake.
questions.a: The second child broke the one-to-one mapping: one shell was paired with two numbers of the standard sequence, so the mapping was not one to one. If a stick had been laid down for each shell, pairing the sticks with the shells afterwards would leave one spare stick and show the error.
s: Names one-to-one mapping as the rule that was broken
Explains that one shell was mapped to two numbers, so the mapping was not one to one
Laying one stick per shell and pairing them back leaves a spare stick, showing the mistake

questions.q: A classmate says: any sequence of symbols can be used as a number system so long as it is long enough. Judge this claim and state the property she has left out.
questions.a: The claim is not acceptable as it stands. The sequence must also have a fixed standard order that everyone follows, and it must be unending, because there is no end to numbers.
s: Says the claim is not acceptable or is incomplete
States that the sequence needs a fixed standard order and must never run out

questions.q: Invent a number system of your own that can count to at least 40 using only two different written symbols in a fixed order. State your rule, write the representation of 7 by that rule, and explain why your system never runs out of symbols.
questions.a: One answer: let a dot stand for 1 and a bar stand for a group of 5. The rule is to write as many bars as there are whole groups of 5, then a dot for each unit left over. Then 7 is one bar and two dots. The system never runs out because bars can simply be repeated, or a third rule can be added, without inventing a new symbol for every number.
s: States two symbols and a clear rule for forming each next representation
Gives the representation of 7 correctly by the rule stated
Explains that the rule can be continued for ever, so no further symbols are needed

concepts.name: Early number systems and counting in groups
concepts.description: Counting with body parts and tally marks, the Gumulgal way of counting in twos, and why counting in groups is more efficient than one mark per object.
concepts.idea: Once people began counting in groups of a fixed size instead of one mark per object, numbers became far quicker to record and to read.
concepts.rule: Count in groups of a chosen size and use one word or symbol for the whole group. The group sizes people have commonly used are 2, 5, 10 and 20.
concepts.example: The Gumulgal counted in twos: urapon is 1, ukasar is 2, and 5 is ukasar-ukasar-urapon, that is 2 + 2 + 1.

questions.q: In the Gumulgal number system of Australia, the word for 1 is
questions.a: urapon

questions.q: Marks cut into a surface such as a bone or a cave wall, one for each object counted, are called ____ marks.
questions.a: tally

questions.q: The Lebombo bone, the oldest known tally stick described in the chapter, carries how many notches?
Which of these group sizes is NOT named in the chapter as one commonly used for counting in groups?
In the Gumulgal system the name for 5 is ukasar-ukasar-urapon because
questions.a: 5 is counted as 2 + 2 + 1
o: the Gumulgal counted in groups of 5

questions.q: Why does the chapter say that counting in twos is more efficient than a tally system?
questions.a: A number is named with far fewer words than a tally needs marks
o: A number is named with far fewer words than a tally needs marks
Tally marks cannot be cut into bone
Counting in twos can name every number, however large
Tally marks have no fixed order

questions.q: Write the Gumulgal names for 4 and for 6, and state what the Gumulgal called any number greater than 6.
questions.a: 4 is ukasar-ukasar and 6 is ukasar-ukasar-ukasar. Any number greater than 6 was simply called ras.
s: Gives 4 as ukasar-ukasar and 6 as ukasar-ukasar-ukasar
States that any number greater than 6 was called ras

questions.q: The Gumulgal of Australia, the Bakairi of South America and the Bushmen of South Africa built equivalent number systems although there is no trace of contact between them. Which explanation does the chapter offer?
questions.a: They may have had common ancestors who used this system, and whose descendants later migrated
o: They may have had common ancestors who used this system, and whose descendants later migrated
They traded with one another across the oceans
All three copied the system from the Romans
Counting in twos is the only system that is possible

questions.q: Most people find it difficult to see the size of a group at a single glance once the group has about how many objects?
questions.a: 5 or more

questions.q: Counting in twos as the Gumulgal did, the number 8 is named by writing ukasar ____ times.
Counting in twos in the Gumulgal way, which number is named ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-urapon?
Extending the Gumulgal system by going on counting in twos, work out (ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-urapon) + (ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-urapon) and give the answer in Gumulgal form.
questions.a: The first name is 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 9 and the second is 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 7, so the sum is 16. Since 16 is eight twos, the answer is ukasar written eight times.
s: Reads the two names as 9 and 7
Writes the sum 16 as ukasar repeated eight times

questions.q: Extending the Gumulgal system by going on counting in twos, work out (ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-urapon) minus (ukasar-ukasar-ukasar) and give the answer in Gumulgal form.
questions.a: The first name is 9 and the second is 6, so the difference is 3. In Gumulgal form 3 is ukasar-urapon.
s: Reads the two names as 9 and 6
Gives the difference 3 as ukasar-urapon

questions.q: A herder cuts one tally mark for each goat and, to make the record easy to read, replaces every group of 5 marks by a new single symbol. For 29 goats his record will show
questions.a: 5 group symbols and 4 single marks
o: 29 single marks and no group symbols

questions.q: A community counts only in groups of 5, with one word for a group of 5 and one word for a single object. Show how they would have to express 1345, and explain why the chapter calls such a system cumbersome.
questions.a: 1345 is exactly 269 groups of 5, since 5 times 269 is 1345, with nothing left over. So the word for a group of 5 would have to be repeated 269 times. A system with only one group size gives no shorter name for a large number, which is why a sequence of larger and larger group sizes is needed.
s: Finds that 1345 is 269 groups of 5 with nothing left over
States that the word for a group of 5 must then be repeated 269 times
Explains that one group size alone gives no short name for a large number

questions.q: Assertion (A): The Lebombo bone is considered one of the oldest mathematical artefacts. Reason (R): It carries 29 notches and is estimated to be about 44,000 years old.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q: Consider: (I) The Gumulgal had a number name for every number. (II) Counting in groups of 2 is one of the group sizes the chapter says people have commonly used. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Only II

questions.q: Two herders keep records on bone. The first cuts one notch for every animal. The second cuts a notch for every animal but replaces each group of 5 notches by a cross. Compare the two records for a herd of 43 animals and say which is easier to read, with a reason.
questions.a: The first record is 43 single notches in a row. The second is 8 crosses and 3 single notches, since 43 is 5 times 8 with 3 left over. The second is far easier to read, because a person cannot take in more than about four marks at a glance, so the grouped record can be read without counting every notch.
s: First record: 43 single notches
Second record: 8 crosses and 3 single notches, since 43 = 5 x 8 + 3
The grouped record is easier, because more than about four marks cannot be seen at a glance

questions.q: A classmate says the Bushmen and the Gumulgal must have traded with each other, because their number systems match. Judge this claim using what the chapter says.
questions.a: The claim is not supported. The chapter says these groups lived far apart with no trace of contact between them. The explanation historians offer is that they may have had common ancestors who used this system and whose descendants migrated to these places.
s: Rejects the claim, since the chapter says there is no trace of contact between the groups
Gives the chapter's explanation: possible common ancestors whose descendants migrated

questions.q: Design a tally system of your own that counts in groups of 4. Give your symbols, show how you would record 30 objects, and state one advantage your system has over single notches.
questions.a: One answer: a stroke for a single object and a square for a group of 4. Since 30 is 4 times 7 with 2 left over, 30 is recorded as 7 squares and 2 strokes. The advantage is that only 9 symbols are read instead of 30, and a small group can be taken in at a glance.
s: States one symbol for a single object and a different symbol for a group of 4
Records 30 as 7 group symbols and 2 single marks, since 30 = 4 x 7 + 2
Gives an advantage: far fewer symbols to read, and small groups are seen at a glance

concepts.name: Roman numerals and landmark numbers
concepts.description: Reading and writing Roman numerals by grouping a number into landmark numbers, the shorter subtractive forms, and why Roman arithmetic is hard.
concepts.idea: Giving a new symbol to a few chosen numbers lets a large number be written with far fewer marks than a tally.
concepts.rule: A number is grouped into as many of the largest landmark number as possible, then the next largest, and so on. The Roman landmark numbers are I 1, V 5, X 10, L 50, C 100, D 500 and M 1000.

questions.q: In the Roman number system the symbol L stands for
The Roman numeral for 1000 is ____.
questions.a: M

questions.q: Numbers such as 1, 5, 10, 50, 100, 500 and 1000, each of which is given a new basic symbol of its own, are called
questions.a: landmark numbers

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a landmark number of the Roman system?
Written as a sum of Roman landmark numbers, XXVII is
Why is 40 usually written as XL rather than as XXXX?
questions.a: XL means 10 less than 50, which is a shorter way of writing 40
o: XL means 10 less than 50, which is a shorter way of writing 40
The symbol L may never be written after X
A Roman symbol is never allowed to be repeated

questions.q: Write 27 and 2367 in Roman numerals.
questions.a: 27 is XXVII. Grouping 2367 as 1000 + 1000 + 100 + 100 + 100 + 50 + 10 + 5 + 1 + 1 gives MMCCCLXVII.
s: Writes 27 as XXVII
Writes 2367 as MMCCCLXVII

questions.q: The number 44 written in Roman numerals, using the shorter forms taught in this chapter, is
questions.a: XLIV

questions.q: The chapter says the Roman system does not lend itself to easy arithmetic. Which operations does it single out as particularly difficult?
questions.a: Multiplication and division

questions.q: Written in Roman numerals, 715 is ____.
questions.a: DCCXV

questions.q: The Roman numeral CCCII stands for
Add CCXXXII and CCCCXIII without converting them into Hindu numerals, and give the answer as a Roman numeral.
questions.a: Counting the symbols together gives 6 Cs, 4 Xs and 5 Is. Five Is regroup to a V, and five of the six Cs regroup to a D, leaving D and C. The four Xs are written XL. So the sum is DCXLV.
s: Collects the symbols as 6 Cs, 4 Xs and 5 Is
Regroups 5 Is as V and 5 Cs as D to get DCXLV

questions.q: Add LXXXVII and LXXVIII in the Roman system and give the answer as a Roman numeral.
questions.a: Together the symbols are 2 Ls, 5 Xs, 2 Vs and 5 Is. The two Ls make C, the five Xs make L, the two Vs make X and the five Is make V. That is C + L + X + V, so the sum is CLXV.
s: Collects the symbols as 2 Ls, 5 Xs, 2 Vs and 5 Is
Regroups them to get CLXV, that is 165

questions.q: Using Roman numerals only, the product V x L is
questions.a: CCL

questions.q: Write 1222 and 302 in Roman numerals, and then explain the rule you used to decide the order in which the symbols are written.
questions.a: 1222 is MCCXXII and 302 is CCCII. The rule is to group the number into as many of the largest landmark number as possible, then as many of the next largest as possible, and so on, and then to write the symbols in that order, largest first.
s: Writes 1222 as MCCXXII
Writes 302 as CCCII
States the rule: group into the largest landmark number first, then the next, and write largest first

questions.q: Assertion (A): The Roman system cannot write larger and larger numbers without introducing more and more new symbols. Reason (R): The Roman system has no symbol for 1000.
questions.a: A is true but R is false
o: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

questions.q: Consider: (I) In the Roman system 2367 is written MMCCCLXVII. (II) In the Roman system a smaller symbol written before a larger one always means the two are to be added. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Only I

questions.q: Sunita adds CCCCXXI and CXIIII by counting symbols and writes the answer as CCCCCXXXV. Her teacher says the value is right but the numeral is not properly written. Explain what is correct, what should be changed, and give the proper numeral.
questions.a: The value is right: five Cs, three Xs and a V come to 500 + 30 + 5, that is 535. What should change is the grouping: five Cs should be written as one D, not as five separate Cs. The proper numeral is DXXXV.
s: Confirms the value: 5 Cs, 3 Xs and a V come to 535
States that 5 Cs regroup to D
Gives the proper numeral DXXXV

questions.q: A classmate writes 99 as IC, saying that it is 1 less than 100. Judge this against the way the chapter forms Roman numerals.
questions.a: It is not acceptable. The chapter forms a numeral by grouping the number into landmark numbers largest first, and uses a shorter subtractive form only just below a landmark number, as in IV for 4 and XL for 40. Grouping 99 gives 90 and 9, so it is written XCIX.
s: Rejects IC as a way of writing 99
Explains the grouping rule and gives XCIX

questions.q: Add one new landmark symbol of your own to the Roman system to stand for 5000, choose a letter for it that is not already in use, and show how 7300 would be written with it. Then explain why the Romans needed new symbols like this as their numbers grew.
questions.a: One answer: let P stand for 5000. Then 7300 is 5000 + 1000 + 1000 + 100 + 100 + 100, which is written PMMCCC. New symbols were needed because the Roman system has no place value, so without a symbol for a larger landmark number, M would have to be repeated again and again for every thousand.
s: Names a new symbol for 5000 that is not already used in the system
Writes 7300 correctly with it, for example PMMCCC
Explains that without new symbols M must be repeated, because the system has no place value

concepts.name: The Egyptian system and the idea of a base
concepts.description: The Egyptian landmark numbers as powers of 10, building a base-5 system in the same way, and the definition of a base-n number system.
concepts.idea: If every landmark number is the same fixed number of times the one before it, the whole sequence of landmark numbers is just the powers of that fixed number.
concepts.rule: A number system is base-n when its first landmark number is 1 and every next landmark number is n times the current one. Its landmark numbers are therefore n to the power 0, n to the power 1, n squared, n cubed, and so on.
concepts.example: The Egyptian landmark numbers are 1, 10, 100, 1000, ... so the Egyptian system is base-10, also called decimal.

questions.q: The landmark numbers of the Egyptian number system are
questions.a: the powers of 10

questions.q: A base-10 number system is also called a ____ number system.
questions.a: decimal

questions.q: A number system whose first landmark number is 1, and in which every next landmark number is got by multiplying the current one by a fixed number n, is called
questions.a: a base-n number system

questions.q: The Egyptian number system described in the chapter was developed around
questions.a: 3000 BCE

questions.q: In the base-5 system built in the chapter, the fourth landmark number is
In the Egyptian system, what makes every landmark number a power of 10?
questions.a: The first landmark number is 1 and each next one is 10 times the previous one
o: The first landmark number is 1 and each next one is 10 times the previous one
The Egyptians had ten fingers to count on
The Egyptians wrote with ten different symbols
10 was the largest number the Egyptians could write

questions.q: List the first five landmark numbers of the base-5 system built in the chapter, and write each one as a power of 5.
questions.a: They are 1, 5, 25, 125 and 625. As powers of 5 these are 5 to the power 0, 5 to the power 1, 5 to the power 2, 5 to the power 3 and 5 to the power 4.
s: Writes them as 5 to the power 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4

questions.q: The landmark numbers of a base-7 system are

How many symbols in all are needed to write 2660 in the Egyptian system?
Express 143 in the base-5 system by grouping it into landmark numbers, and say how many of each landmark number are needed.
questions.a: Starting from the largest landmark number not more than 143, we get 143 = 125 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 1 + 1 + 1. So it needs one 125, no 25s, three 5s and three 1s.
s: States one 125, no 25s, three 5s and three 1s

questions.q: Write 651 as a sum of the landmark numbers of the base-5 system, taking as many of the largest landmark number as possible at each step.
questions.a: The largest landmark number not more than 651 is 625, and 651 - 625 = 26. The largest landmark number not more than 26 is 25, and 26 - 25 = 1. So 651 = 625 + 25 + 1.
s: Begins with 625, the largest landmark number not more than 651

questions.q: Grouped into the landmark numbers of the base-5 system, the number 137 needs
questions.a: one 125, two 5s and two 1s

questions.q: Represent 10458 in the Egyptian system by grouping it into landmark numbers, and state how many symbols the numeral needs altogether.
questions.a: Grouping largest first, 10458 = 10000 + 400 + 50 + 8. That is one ten-thousand symbol, four hundred symbols, five ten symbols and eight unit strokes. Altogether the numeral needs 1 + 4 + 5 + 8 = 18 symbols.
s: States one ten-thousand symbol, four hundred symbols, five ten symbols and eight unit strokes
Gives the total as 18 symbols

questions.q: Assertion (A): 25 is the second landmark number of the base-5 system built in the chapter. Reason (R): In a base-5 system every landmark number after the first is 5 times the previous one.
questions.a: A is false but R is true
o: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
